metaTitle: Bugs That Look Like Bed Bugs: How to Tell Apart
metaDescription: Bat bugs, carpet beetle larvae, spider beetles, booklice, fleas and ticks pass for bed bugs. See the clues that separate them and how to get an ID.
h1: Bugs That Look Like Bed Bugs: Eight Look-Alikes and How to Tell Them Apart
dek: How to separate a real bed bug from eight insects commonly mistaken for one, using the clues in government and university sources, and how to get a specimen identified when you cannot tell.
excerpt: Eight bugs often get mistaken for bed bugs: bat bugs, swallow bugs, carpet beetle larvae, spider beetles, booklice, cockroach nymphs, fleas and ticks. How to tell each one apart.

quickAnswer.lead: **Bat bugs, swallow bugs, carpet beetle larvae, spider beetles, booklice, cockroach nymphs, fleas and ticks are bugs commonly mistaken for bed bugs.** A real adult bed bug is about the size of an apple seed and flat and oval, with wings it does not use for flying, as the [EPA's bed bug appearance page](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle) describes.
bullets: An adult bed bug is 3/16 to 1/4 inch (5 to 7 mm) long and does not jump or fly, so a bug that hops or flies is something else.
A bed bug has 6 legs and a tick has 8, so a leg count separates the two.
Bat bugs have fringe hairs behind the head that are longer than the width of the eyes, while a bed bug's hairs are shorter.
Spider beetles are about 1/16 to 1/8 inch (2 to 4 mm) long with a globe-shaped abdomen.
Bat bugs and bird-feeding bugs can bite people but cannot reproduce on human blood.
Bites alone cannot confirm or rule out bed bugs, so an identified specimen is the reliable check.

body.text: Which bugs get mistaken for bed bugs?

Bat bugs, swallow bugs, carpet beetle larvae, spider beetles, booklice, cockroach nymphs, fleas and ticks are look-alikes that commonly pass for bed bugs. [NC State Extension](https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/tips-for-preventing-the-spread-of-bedbugs) says German cockroach nymphs, carpet beetles, ticks and booklice are mistaken for bed bugs all the time. The two closest matches are bat bugs and swallow bugs, relatives of the bed bug that feed on bats and birds, which [Colorado State University's look-alike page](https://agsci.colostate.edu/agbio/ipm-pests/bed-bug-look-alikes) covers.

Getting the identification right comes first. The [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle) calls an accurate identification a critical first step toward avoiding costly treatment for the wrong bug. This guide uses the real bed bug as the yardstick, sorts each look-alike by the clues the sources give, and ends with how to get a specimen identified. If the insect does turn out to be a bed bug, the [complete US guide to bed bugs](/learn/bed-bugs) covers biology, inspection and every treatment option.

body.text: What does a real bed bug look like?

An adult bed bug is about the size of an apple seed, 3/16 to 1/4 inch (5 to 7 mm) long, and flat and oval when it has not fed. The [EPA's bed bug appearance page](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle) describes it as brown before a meal and reddish-brown, more elongated and balloon-like after one, with a three-segment beak, four-part antennae, wings that are not used for flying and short golden hairs. The [Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station's identification poster](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/bed_bugs/bedbugsandlookalikes11x17pdf.pdf?rev=b5eda78591fe46fba25609c37873f96b&hash=AB5D5C40AB6B05BD6CE38B7285EE0946) gives the same size as about 1/4 inch and adds that bed bugs walk: they do not jump, fly or hop.

Young bed bugs are far smaller than adults. The EPA lists the five nymph stages at about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm) for the first, then 2, 2.5 and 3 mm, and about 3/16 inch (4.5 mm) for the fifth, and describes the eggs as pearl-white and the size of a pinhead. [What baby bed bugs look like at every stage](/blog/baby-bed-bugs-nymphs) shows each one, and [what bed bugs look like](/blog/what-do-bed-bugs-look-like) covers the adult in more detail.

items: **Legs.** A bed bug has 6 legs, and NC State uses the leg count to separate bed bugs from ticks, which have 8.
**Movement.** It walks. A bug that hops is not a bed bug, and neither is one that flies.
**Shape.** Broadly oval and flat from top to bottom, which the Connecticut station calls dorsally flat.
**Antennae.** Four segments according to the EPA, with the last segment nearly half the length of the one before it, as Colorado State describes.
**Habits.** The Connecticut station says bed bugs do not live on people; they hide elsewhere and commute to feed.

body.text: How can you tell the look-alikes apart at a glance?

Count the legs, check whether the bug hops or flies, then look at its hair and body shape; the table pairs each clue with the look-alike it points to. Treat it as a sorting aid, because several of these insects can only be separated for certain under magnification.

body.text: How do you tell a bat bug or swallow bug from a bed bug?

Usually only under magnification, because bat bugs and swallow bugs are red- or gray-brown and wingless like bed bugs, and the differences are in the hairs and the antennae. [Colorado State University's look-alike page](https://agsci.colostate.edu/agbio/ipm-pests/bed-bug-look-alikes) says the three share the color and the lack of wings, and it separates them by hair length and antennal segments.
Bat bugs

A bat bug has fringe hairs just behind the head that are longer than the width of its eyes, while a bed bug's are shorter than the width of its eyes, according to the same page. Judging a hair against an eye on an insect this small takes magnification, which is why a doubtful bug is a job for an identification service rather than a quick look.

Location is the second clue. Colorado State places bat bugs in attics, between walls, in chimneys and under shingles, close to the bats they feed on. The page also says bat bugs and bird-feeding bugs can bite people but cannot reproduce on human blood, so a bat bug found in a bedroom points to bats in the building as the source. To compare that with where real infestations sit, see [where bed bugs hide](/blog/where-do-bed-bugs-hide), which ranks hiding places by distance from the bed.
Swallow bugs

A swallow bug (*Oeciacus vicarius*) is a bed bug relative that feeds on cliff and barn swallows and lives in cliff swallow mud nests on natural and man-made structures. Its tell is the antennae: the last two segments are nearly equal in length, while a bed bug's last two are unequal and its last segment is nearly half the length of the one before it. Colorado State says swallow bugs are more likely to bite people in spring, before the swallows return to their nests, or in autumn, after the birds have abandoned them.
How do carpet beetles and their larvae differ from bed bugs?

Carpet beetle larvae are hairy and segmented and lack both the flat shape and the distinct head of a bed bug. The [Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station's poster](https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/caes/documents/bed_bugs/bedbugsandlookalikes11x17pdf.pdf?rev=b5eda78591fe46fba25609c37873f96b&hash=AB5D5C40AB6B05BD6CE38B7285EE0946) pairs a larva with an adult bed bug to show the difference, noting that the larva's hairy, segmented body can resemble a bed bug's abdomen. [NC State](https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/tips-for-preventing-the-spread-of-bedbugs) puts it as much hairier and not flat.

The adults are easier to rule out. The Connecticut poster says carpet beetle larvae develop into winged adult beetles, and NC State says the adults differ from bed bugs in shape and color but are still regularly mistaken for them. A beetle that flies is not a bed bug, since the EPA says bed bug wings are not used for flying.

On skin, the Connecticut poster's point is that hairs of the varied carpet beetle can irritate skin. Irritation from hairs is a different thing from a bite, and a rash alone cannot tell you which insect is present. For the small dark bugs that get confused with bed bugs, carpet beetles included, see [why a bed bug can look nearly black](/blog/black-bed-bugs).
How do spider beetles, booklice and cockroach nymphs compare?

Spider beetles have a globe-shaped rear and some species fly, booklice are soft-bodied with a bulging face, and cockroach nymphs have their own identification guides. All three get brought in as suspected bed bugs.
Spider beetles

Spider beetles are about 1/16 to 1/8 inch (2 to 4 mm) long, smaller than an adult bed bug, with a globular abdomen, a head turned down so it is hidden from above, and thin legs and antennae. [Colorado State University Extension's spider beetle fact sheet](https://wci.extension.colostate.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/14/2017/03/SpiderBeetlesJan42010.pdf) says most species are brown to reddish-brown and covered in fine hairs or scales, and that the family name comes from the most globe-shaped, least hairy species, which superficially resemble spiders.

They are scavengers. The fact sheet lists seeds, grain debris, herbs, dried fruit and fungi, along with feathers and dead insects, and says they may develop in rodent nest refuse; it does not describe them feeding on blood or biting people. In Colorado, most species need fairly high humidity, so they turn up in damp basements and crawl spaces. Flight is another separator: males of the whitemarked spider beetle can fly, and in some other species both sexes can, while the EPA says bed bug wings are not used for flying.

Two relatives, the drugstore beetle and the cigarette beetle, share the downturned head and humped body. The fact sheet says they have serrated or clubbed antennae and are good fliers that are drawn to lights.

body.text: Booklice

Booklice are the soft-bodied option. NC State describes them as softer-bodied insects, light tan in color, with a bulging face, which sets them apart from the flat, oval, brown bed bug the EPA describes. The sources used for this guide do not give booklice sizes or feeding habits, so a specimen is the safe way to settle a doubtful one.
Cockroach nymphs

NC State lists German cockroach nymphs among the insects mistaken for bed bugs all the time. Separating them is a topic of its own: [what baby cockroaches look like](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) covers nymphs of the common species and how they differ from bed bugs and beetles, and [whether cockroaches bite](/blog/do-cockroaches-bite) covers what is documented about bites.
How do you tell fleas and ticks from bed bugs?
Fleas hop and ticks have eight legs, and a bed bug does neither, so both are usually easy to rule out once you can see one clearly.
Fleas

The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station describes adult fleas as laterally flat, meaning narrow from side to side, with powerful hind legs and the ability to jump. A bed bug is flat from top to bottom and walks. The same poster says flea larvae look like small clear worms and are more likely to be found in pet bedding than in mattresses, which is a good reason to check where any pets sleep. What flea bites on people look like is covered in [flea bites on humans and how to tell them apart](/blog/flea-bites-on-humans).
Ticks

Count the legs. NC State says a tick has 8 and a bed bug has 6, which is the quickest way to separate the two. A tick on a person or pet is a different matter from a household pest: [how to tell a tick from a bed bug](/blog/tick-vs-bed-bug) compares the two, and [what ticks look like](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like) shows the life stages. Contact a healthcare provider, or a veterinarian for a pet, if you are worried about a tick bite.
Could it be lint, a seed or lice instead of a bug?

Yes. The Connecticut poster notes that seeds and lint can look remarkably similar to insects with the naked eye, and it shows an elm seed, a wood sorrel seed and a clump of lint for comparison. A hand lens or microscope settles it. The poster also lists lice, which it describes as long, tear-shaped insects that live on people or in their clothing and cannot live long away from a human host, although they can occasionally turn up on the mattresses of heavily infested people. A healthcare provider can confirm lice.
Can you identify the bug from the bites?

No. NC State Extension advises against using bites, whether present or absent, to identify a bed bug infestation or to rule one out. The look-alikes show why: bat bugs and swallow bugs can bite people, and hairs of the varied carpet beetle can irritate skin, so a rash cannot tell you which insect is responsible. For what bed bug bites typically look like, see [bed bug bites: what they look like and how long they last](/blog/bed-bug-bites). Contact a healthcare provider about any reaction that worries you.
How do you get a specimen identified by an extension office?

Catch the bug, keep it intact in a small container, and take or send it to your state's cooperative extension office or its insect diagnostic lab. The [EPA's bed bug page](https://www.epa.gov/bedbugs/bed-bugs-appearance-and-life-cycle) says a state cooperative extension service office may be able to help with identification, and [NC State](https://content.ces.ncsu.edu/tips-for-preventing-the-spread-of-bedbugs) advises reaching out to a diagnostician when you have doubts.

Services differ by state: North Carolina residents are told to send samples to NC State's Plant Disease and Insect Clinic, while the University of Wisconsin-Madison's Insect Diagnostic Lab does not accept physical specimens shipped from out of state and directs those senders to their local extension office or a university entomology department. Search your state's land-grant university for an insect diagnostic page, or call the county extension office and ask where specimens go.

items: Photograph the bug first, with a coin beside it for scale. The [University of Wisconsin-Madison Insect Diagnostic Lab](https://insectlab.russell.wisc.edu/samples) says insects can be identified from digital images in many cases, but in other cases a physical specimen must be inspected under a microscope.

Collect the whole insect without crushing it. The Connecticut station's list of inspection equipment includes a bright flashlight, a hand lens, latex gloves, soft forceps and a glass bottle to hold insects for identification.
For a hard-bodied insect such as a beetle or true bug, Wisconsin's lab says a dry specimen in a small clean vial or box with cotton or tissue for cushioning works.

For a soft-bodied specimen, which Wisconsin illustrates with aphids, caterpillars and worms, use alcohol: 70 percent ethanol is best, and rubbing alcohol or clear 80-proof liquor will work. The lab says soft-bodied insects left dry can decompose and become unidentifiable within days, and it advises pouring off the excess alcohol and adding a cotton ball before mailing.
Do not use tape on the specimen. Wisconsin warns that tape can make identification difficult.

Add where and when you found it and anything the lab's form asks for. Wisconsin says background information sent with an image or specimen can greatly assist the diagnosis and offers a printable form for it, and a lab's own instructions win wherever they differ from this list.

body.title: Photo or specimen?
body.text: A photo can be enough for many insects, but the bat bug and swallow bug differences depend on hair length against eye width and on antennal proportions. When either is possible, send the physical specimen.
What should you do once you know what you have?

If the answer is a bed bug, check the bed first and follow a full plan. [What bed bug signs on a mattress look like and what to do about them](/blog/bed-bugs-on-mattress) is the place to start, and [the complete bed bug elimination plan](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-bed-bugs) covers confirming, containing and treating an infestation.

If the answer is a look-alike, the fix belongs to that insect, not to a bed bug plan. A bat bug or swallow bug points to bats or birds using the building, and a carpet beetle, spider beetle, flea or tick each has its own guide or an extension office that can advise. Read any pesticide label in full before using the product, because the label is the law.

faqs.question: Can bat bugs live in my bed like bed bugs?
faqs.answer: Not the way bed bugs do. Colorado State University's look-alike page says bat bugs and bird-feeding bugs can bite people but cannot reproduce on human blood. Bat bugs parasitize bats and are found in attics, between walls, in chimneys and under shingles, so one in a bedroom points to bats in the building as the source. The page separates them from bed bugs by hair length behind the head, which makes a doubtful insect a case for an extension diagnostician.

faqs.question: Do bed bugs fly or jump?
faqs.answer: No. The EPA's bed bug page says a bed bug's wings are not used for flying, and the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station says bed bugs do not jump, fly or hop; they walk. An insect that hops is more likely a flea, which the Connecticut station describes as laterally flat with powerful hind legs. A winged insect that flies is something else, such as a carpet beetle adult or one of the spider beetle species in which flight occurs.

faqs.question: Can I identify a bug from a photo?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. The University of Wisconsin-Madison Insect Diagnostic Lab says insects can be identified from digital images in many cases, but in other cases a physical specimen must be inspected under a microscope. Bat bugs and swallow bugs are likely to need the specimen, because Colorado State describes the differences as hair length against eye width and the proportions of the antennal segments, and says the bat bug's hair feature is only visible with magnification. If you send a photo, keep it in focus with a coin beside the insect, and keep the bug itself in case the lab asks.

faqs.question: When do swallow bugs bite people?
faqs.answer: Colorado State University says swallow bugs are more likely to bite people in spring, before swallows return to their nests, or in autumn, after the swallows have abandoned a nest. Swallow bugs live in cliff swallow mud nests on natural or man-made structures, which includes buildings. They are told from bed bugs by the antennae: the last two segments are nearly equal in length, while in a bed bug they are not.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether the bug is dead or alive when I submit it?
faqs.answer: The sources used here do not say a live insect is required. The University of Wisconsin-Madison lab accepts hard-bodied insects dry in a small clean vial or box, and it asks that soft-bodied insects be preserved in alcohol, with 70 percent ethanol best. It advises against tape. The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station lists a spray bottle of soapy water to disable or kill insects and a glass bottle to hold them for identification. Check your own lab's instructions first.
